title: Borelli v. Brusseau
lead: A wife alleged that her husband promised property if she personally cared for him at home after a stroke; the majority treated that care as an existing marital duty, while the dissent would allow her to prove an additional bargain.

actors.name: Hildegard Borelli
actors.role: Wife seeking performance of an alleged promise for home care

actors.name: Michael Borelli
actors.role: Husband who allegedly promised estate property before his death

actors.name: Monique Lee
actors.role: Michael’s stepdaughter included in the promised education and insurance benefits

proceedings: Complaint dismissed after demurrer sustained without leave to amend; Court of Appeal affirmed 2–1 with costs to respondents; rehearing and state Supreme Court review were later denied, with Kennard voting for review.
limits: The alleged bargain and performance were assumed for pleading, not found after trial. The antenuptial agreement’s text was absent. The historical marital-duty ruling did not categorically forbid spouses’ property contracts or adjudicate every writing requirement.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The marriage and earlier estate discussions preceded the alleged exchange
sections.cue: Identify the promised interests without collapsing them into real property alone.
paragraphs: Hildegard and Michael Borelli signed an antenuptial agreement on April 24, 1980 and married the next day. Michael was hospitalized for heart problems in March 1983, February 1984, and January 1987. Worried about health and longevity, he said he intended to leave Hildegard specified property and benefits: an interest in a Sacramento lot, a life estate in a Hawaiian condominium, a quarter interest in Borelli Meat Co., remaining bank cash, his interest in a Kensington residence and furniture, a partnership interest, and health insurance for Hildegard and his stepdaughter Monique Lee, along with Monique’s education expenses.

Those earlier statements provided background. After a stroke in August 1988, Michael repeatedly said during hospitalization and rehabilitation that he disliked being away and did not want nursing-home care. Remaining home required constant care and house modifications, while doctors recommended a rest home or convalescent hospital.

Around October, he allegedly promised the listed property, including a full interest in the Sacramento property, in return for Hildegard personally caring for him at home throughout illness. She alleged complete performance in their confidential marital relationship. Michael died January 25, 1989. His will instead gave her $100,000 and his interest in their jointly held residence, leaving most of the estate to his daughter Brusseau, who served as executor.

sections.title: The complaint failed before any trial of the promise
sections.cue: Establish the pleading posture and missing antenuptial terms.
paragraphs: Hildegard sought specific performance against the estate interests. The trial court sustained a demurrer without leave to amend and dismissed. On appeal, the court accepted properly pleaded material allegations but did not treat new assertions in briefing as established facts. It therefore addressed whether the alleged personal care could supply consideration and whether public policy permitted the bargain, not whether Michael actually made it.

The complaint mentioned the antenuptial agreement but did not supply its text. The court did not construe its terms or determine every promised asset’s value. Justice Poché would infer substantial separate property in dissent, but that inference was not an adjudicated interpretation of the missing instrument.

sections.title: The majority classified personal nursing as support already owed
sections.cue: Explain the duty and the response to unequal-treatment objections.
paragraphs: Justice Perley, joined by Presiding Justice Anderson, emphasized marriage as a legally regulated status. The Civil Code required reciprocal support, respect, fidelity, and support while cohabiting, while separately permitting property transactions between spouses. In the majority’s view, the latter permission did not allow contracting away personal obligations of marital status.

Estate of Sonnicksen and Brooks v. Brooks, earlier spousal-care decisions, treated nursing an ill spouse as an existing duty. A promise of compensation for that performance supplied no new consideration and offended public policy. Hildegard argued that those cases imposed outdated gender roles by allowing husbands to pay support while requiring wives to nurse personally. The majority answered that the obligation was reciprocal and later decisions applied it to both spouses.

It used consortium authorities to identify companionship, affection, comfort, and physical household assistance beyond money. Watkins permitted compensation for premarital homemaking but did not extend it to marital support. Vincent, an assistance-program decision, treated an existing marital duty as a valid basis for denying payment while requiring equal treatment of spouses. These supported the majority’s conception without themselves deciding Hildegard’s contract.

Support’s personal elements made it nondelegable in a way comparable to fidelity and respect. Accordingly, her alleged full performance supplied no additional consideration. Marital rights including community-property rights remained, and spouses still could make valid property agreements on other subjects.

sections.title: Public policy reinforced the pre-existing-duty conclusion
sections.cue: Keep the fraud concern separate from a finding against Hildegard.
paragraphs: The majority acknowledged that age alone did not justify retaining a rule. It nevertheless considered the duty gender neutral and saw continuing risks of fabricated compensation agreements after care had been rendered. It did not find Hildegard fraudulent or say fraud risk alone explained everything.

It also rejected the dissent’s suggestion that nonenforcement might encourage a spouse to leave and bargain for return. The majority considered sickbed price negotiations inconsistent with marriage’s statutory personal-support obligations. Thus both lack of new consideration and public policy supported dismissal even assuming the promised care had been fully performed.

sections.title: Poché distinguished ensuring care from personally supplying all nursing
sections.cue: Present the dissent’s alternative legal account and reserved issues.
paragraphs: Justice Poché accepted a duty of support and medical care but denied that each spouse must personally perform every nursing service. Older precedent reflected coverture and a division of male financial support and female domestic labor. Modern reciprocal duties, employment, and household arrangements allowed professional help, other assistance, or relatives to provide care. A promise to perform personally at home could therefore add something valuable.

Statutory permission for property transactions and retreat from interspousal tort and contract immunity supported enforcement. His first note also discussed abandonment of parental immunity. Michael could buy the same services from a stranger; marriage should not erase consideration when Hildegard chose to supply them herself.

Poché would let courts hear evidence of existence or fraud rather than prohibit the category. Fraud was not proved at demurrer. His second note declined to resolve possible statute-of-frauds and property-transmutation problems because the complaint alleged defendants were estopped to invoke them. That did not establish that the oral bargain satisfied every statutory formality.

He contrasted enforceable reconciliation agreements after separation. From alleged abandonment of independent living, he inferred that Hildegard might otherwise have left; the majority called that speculation. He thought it perverse if separation improved the ability to bargain for conduct preserving marriage. Although sickbed negotiations could be unsettling, compelled altruism did not establish a sufficient legal policy. He would permit an effort to prove the agreement.

sections.title: The dismissal stood without a factual finding that the bargain was false
sections.cue: Close with the vote and limited later procedural notations.
paragraphs: On January 19, 1993, the court affirmed dismissal two to one and awarded respondents costs. It neither transferred the promised assets nor compensated nursing services nor found the allegations false.

The report records rehearing denied February 17 and California Supreme Court review denied April 1, with Justice Kennard voting to grant review. Those denials were not a state Supreme Court merits opinion adopting every part of the majority’s reasoning.
